items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.

items.title: Your average speed never equals your speed at most moments
items.claim: Drive 60 miles in one hour at varying speeds — slowing for lights, accelerating onto highways. Average speed is 60 mph. But that doesn't mean you were doing 60 mph for most of the time. You may have spent more time at 30 mph than at 90 mph.
items.prompt: What's the difference between average and instantaneous?

options.text: Average and instantaneous are equal at the midpoint

Average speed = total distance / total time. Instantaneous speed = the limit of average speed over a vanishing interval — the derivative dx/dt. The mean value theorem guarantees at SOME instant the instantaneous speed equals the average, but not at most or all instants

items.reveal:
Mean Value Theorem (MVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a).

In driving terms: at SOME moment during your journey, your instantaneous speed was exactly equal to your average speed. (Not all moments — at least one.) This is the rigorous version of what intuition gets right.

Applications:
- Speed cameras using 'average speed enforcement': measure entry and exit times over a stretch; if average exceeds limit, you must have exceeded the limit at SOME moment (MVT). This is legally watertight.
- Optimisation: locating extrema where f'(c) = 0.
- L'Hopital's rule and Taylor's theorem are MVT consequences.

The full Taylor expansion exploits this: f(b) = f(a) + f'(a)(b-a) + (1/2)f''(a)(b-a)^2 + ... Each term corrects the linear approximation with higher-order behaviour. The remainder terms involve derivatives at intermediate points (Lagrange remainder).

Derivative as instantaneous rate: dx/dt at t = t_0 is the limit as h approaches 0 of (x(t_0 + h) - x(t_0)) / h. Defined when this limit exists. It tells you the rate of change exactly at time t_0 — not over any finite interval.

Velocity (vector) vs speed (scalar magnitude). At a U-turn, average velocity over the round trip is zero (you end up back where you started), but average speed is non-zero. Distinguishing them is key in kinematics.
items.why: Average rates feel like reliable summaries of what happened. The mean value theorem guarantees only ONE instant matches the average; for most of a journey, instantaneous speed differs. Speed limits use both.

items.title: Switching doors doubles your chance of the car
items.claim: Three doors, one car, two goats. Pick a door. Monty (who knows where the car is) opens a different door revealing a goat. Should you switch?
items.prompt: What's the probability of winning if you switch?

options.text: 1/3 — first guess was 1/3, opening a door doesn't change anything
2/3 — your first guess had 1/3 chance of being right, so the remaining unopened door now carries the original 2/3 probability of the OTHER two doors combined
100 percent — Monty's reveal guarantees the win

items.reveal_title: Marilyn vos Savant and a thousand wrong PhDs
items.reveal:
Vos Savant published the answer 'switch' in Parade magazine in 1990. Thousands of readers wrote in — including PhDs in mathematics — insisting she was wrong. She was right.

The key: Monty knows where the car is and always reveals a goat. Your initial choice has 1/3 probability of the car. The OTHER two doors together have 2/3 probability. Monty's reveal removes one of those two doors but doesn't change the 2/3 — it now sits entirely on the remaining unopened door.

If Monty acted randomly (sometimes revealing the car himself), switching wouldn't help — but he doesn't. His knowledge is essential.

The Monty Hall puzzle is the canonical demonstration that conditional probability defeats intuition. Run the simulation 1000 times: switching wins about 667 of them, sticking wins 333.
items.why: Probability intuition assumes 'two outcomes equally likely'. Conditional probability — conditioning on what Monty reveals — distinguishes outcomes that 'look' symmetric but aren't.
